body.en:
Data are raw facts and figures, such as numbers, characters, names or marks, that have no meaning on their own. Example: 67, 82, 45, 91.

Information is data that has been processed (organised, calculated, compared) so that it has a meaning and is useful for decisions. Example: "Sara is the topper with 91 marks; class average is 71.25".

DataInformation
Raw, unorganised factsProcessed, organised data
No meaning by itselfMeaningful and useful
Input to processingOutput of processing
Example: list of marksExample: result, rank, average

Related terms

  • Data item / field: a single unit of value, e.g. roll number.
  • Group item: a data item made of sub-items, e.g. name = first name + last name.
  • Record: a collection of related fields about one entity, e.g. one student's roll no, name and marks.
  • File: a collection of records of the same type, e.g. all students of a class.
  • Entity: something that has attributes, e.g. student. Attribute: a property of the entity, e.g. age.

A data structure is a particular way of organising, storing and managing data in memory so that it can be used (accessed and modified) efficiently.

In short: Data Structure = organised data + allowed operations.

Niklaus Wirth summed it up as: Algorithms + Data Structures = Programs.

Need for data structures

  • Efficient processing: a good structure makes searching, inserting and deleting faster. Example: searching a sorted array with binary search takes about 20 comparisons for 10 lakh items, while linear search may take 10 lakh.
  • Large amounts of data: real applications (banking, railway reservation, social media) handle millions of records that must be organised.
  • Proper use of memory: structures like linked lists use memory only when needed.
  • Reusability: a stack or queue, once written, can be used in many programs.
  • Abstraction: the user works with operations (push, pop) without worrying about how they are stored.

Real-life examples

  • Stack: pile of plates, undo in an editor, browser back button.
  • Queue: ticket counter line, printer jobs, CPU scheduling.
  • Tree: folders on a computer, family tree, organisation chart.
  • Graph: road map (Google Maps), friends on social media, computer networks.

h.en: 1.1.3 Types of Data Structures: Primitive and Non-Primitive

body.en:
Data structures are classified as shown in the diagram.

1. Primitive data structures

  • Basic data types that are directly operated upon by machine instructions.
  • Each holds a single value.
  • Examples: int, float, double, char, pointer.
  • Their size depends on the machine and compiler (e.g. int = 2 bytes in Turbo C, 4 bytes in GCC).

2. Non-primitive data structures

  • Derived from primitive data structures.
  • Store a group of values (homogeneous or heterogeneous) and the relationship between them.
  • Examples: arrays, stacks, queues, linked lists, trees, graphs, files.
  • They are further divided into linear and non-linear data structures.
PrimitiveNon-primitive
Basic, built-in typesDerived from primitive types
Hold a single valueHold a collection of values
Operated directly by the CPUOperated through algorithms
Fixed sizeSize may be fixed or dynamic
int, float, char, double, pointerArray, stack, queue, list, tree, graph

Linear data structure

Elements are arranged in a sequence, one after another. Every element (except the first and the last) has exactly one predecessor and one successor. Elements can be traversed in a single run.

Examples: array, stack, queue, linked list.

Non-linear data structure

Elements are arranged in a hierarchical or network manner. One element can be connected to several other elements, so they cannot be traversed in a single run.

Examples: tree, graph.

LinearNon-linear
Elements in a sequenceElements in a hierarchy or network
Each element has at most one predecessor and one successorAn element may be linked to many elements
Single levelMultiple levels
Traversed in a single runNeeds special traversals (inorder, BFS, DFS…)
Easy to implementMore complex to implement
Memory may be wasted (array)Memory used efficiently
Array, stack, queue, linked listTree, graph

Static and dynamic data structures

  • Static: size fixed at compile time, e.g. array.
  • Dynamic: size can grow or shrink at run time, e.g. linked list.

The following operations are performed on almost every data structure:

  1. Traversing: accessing each element exactly once to process it (print, count, sum).
  2. Searching: finding the location of an element with a given value (key).
  3. Insertion: adding a new element.
  4. Deletion: removing an existing element.
  5. Sorting: arranging elements in ascending or descending order.
  6. Merging: combining the elements of two structures into one.

Some structures allow these operations only in a restricted way. In a stack, insertion (push) and deletion (pop) happen only at the top. In a queue, insertion is at the rear and deletion at the front.

The choice of data structure depends on which operations are needed most often. For example, arrays give fast access by index, while linked lists give fast insertion and deletion.

An algorithm is a finite sequence of well-defined steps for solving a particular problem. It takes some input, processes it, and produces the required output in a finite amount of time.

The word comes from the name of the Persian mathematician al-Khwarizmi.

Conventions used in GTU-style algorithms

  • Name of the algorithm with its parameters: Algorithm MAX(A, N).
  • Numbered steps: Step 1, Step 2, …, each with a comment in [ ] brackets.
  • Assignment with Set or ←: Set MAX = A[0].
  • Decision: If condition then … [End of If].
  • Loop: Repeat for I = 1 to N or Repeat while condition.
  • Input/Output: Read, Write / Print; and Exit at the end.

Example: largest of N numbers

Algorithm MAX(A, N)
A = array of N elements, MAX = largest
Step 1: [Initialize]  Set MAX = A[0]
Step 2: [Loop]  Repeat for I = 1 to N-1
            If A[I] > MAX then
                Set MAX = A[I]
        [End of loop]
Step 3: [Output]  Print MAX
Step 4: Exit

Algorithm vs program

AlgorithmProgram
Step-by-step solution in simple languageImplementation of the algorithm in a programming language
Independent of language and machineDepends on the language (C, Python…)
Written at the design stageWritten at the implementation stage
Must terminate (finite)May run forever (e.g. an OS)
Analysed for time and spaceTested and executed

Every algorithm must have the following five properties (see diagram):

  1. Input: it takes zero or more inputs from outside.
  2. Output: it produces at least one output (result).
  3. Definiteness: each step is clear and unambiguous; it has only one meaning. "Add a few numbers" is not definite; "add A and B" is.
  4. Finiteness: the algorithm must terminate after a finite number of steps for every input. A loop with no end condition breaks this rule.
  5. Effectiveness: every step must be basic enough to be carried out exactly, in a finite time, using pencil and paper.

Other desirable properties:

  • Correctness: gives the right output for every valid input.
  • Generality: works for all inputs of the problem, not just one case.
  • Efficiency: uses as little time and memory as possible.
  • Language independence: can be coded in any language.

h.en: 1.2.3 Analysis of an Algorithm: Best, Worst and Average Case

body.en:
Analysis of an algorithm means estimating the resources (time and memory) it needs, as a function of the input size n. It helps us choose the best of several algorithms for the same problem.

Two approaches

  • A priori analysis (theoretical): done before running, by counting steps. Independent of machine and language. This is what we use.
  • A posteriori analysis (empirical): run the program and measure the actual time. Depends on the machine, compiler and load.

Three cases

The running time often depends not only on n but also on the arrangement of the input. Example: linear search for a key in n elements.

  • Best case: the minimum time, for the most favourable input. Key found at the first position → 1 comparison → O(1).
  • Worst case: the maximum time, for the most unfavourable input. Key at the last position or absent → n comparisons → O(n).
  • Average case: the expected time over all inputs. Key equally likely anywhere → about (n + 1)/2 comparisons → O(n).

The worst case is usually the most important, because it gives a guarantee: the algorithm will never take longer than this.

title.en: 1.3 Time Complexity, Space Complexity and Asymptotic Notations

body.en:
The time complexity of an algorithm is the amount of time it needs to run to completion, expressed as a function of the input size n. We do not measure seconds (they depend on the machine). Instead we count the number of basic operations (comparisons, assignments, additions) executed.

Frequency count (step count) method

Count how many times each statement executes, then add them up. Keep only the highest-order term and drop constants to get the Big O.

Example 1: sum of an array → O(n)

int sum(int a[], int n)
{
    /* 1          */
    int s = 0, i;
    /* n + 1 tests */
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
        /* n          */
        s = s + a[i];
    /* 1          */
    return s;
/* total 2n+3 */
}

Total = 1 + (n + 1) + n + 1 = 2n + 3 → O(n).

Example 2: nested loops → O(n²)

/* outer: n   */
for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
    /* inner: n   */
    for (j = 0; j < n; j++)
        /* n x n = n2 */
        c = c + 1;

Example 3: loop variable doubles → O(log n)

i = 1;
while (i < n)        /* i = 1,2,4,8 ... */
    /* runs log2(n) times */
    i = i * 2;

Example 4: no loop → O(1)

int square(int x)
{
    /* always 1 step: O(1) */
    return x * x;
}

Common complexities (fastest to slowest)

Big ONameExample
O(1)ConstantAccess a[i], push/pop
O(log n)LogarithmicBinary search
O(n)LinearLinear search, traversal
O(n log n)LinearithmicMerge sort, quick sort (avg)
O(n²)QuadraticBubble, selection, insertion sort
O(2ⁿ)ExponentialRecursive Fibonacci

The space complexity of an algorithm is the amount of memory it needs to run to completion, as a function of the input size n.

Space needed S(P) = Fixed part (c) + Variable part (Sp)

  • Fixed part: independent of the input size. Space for the code (instructions), simple variables, constants and fixed-size structures.
  • Variable part: depends on the input size. Space for arrays of size n, dynamically allocated memory, and the recursion stack (each recursive call needs space for its parameters, local variables and return address).

Example 1: constant space → O(1)

int add(int a, int b)
{
    int c = a + b;   /* a, b, c: fixed */
    return c;        /* S(P) = c -> O(1) */
}

Example 2: space grows with n → O(n)

int total(int a[], int n)
{
    int i, s = 0;    /* fixed: i, s, n  */
    for (i = 0; i < n; i++)
        s += a[i];   /* a[] : n words    */
    /* S(P) = n + 3 = O(n) */
    return s;
}

The array needs n words; i, s and n need 3 words. S(P) = n + 3 → O(n).

Time–space trade-off

Often we can make an algorithm faster by using more memory, or save memory at the cost of time. Example: a lookup table of pre-computed squares answers in O(1) time but needs O(n) extra space.

h.en: 1.3.3 Asymptotic Notations: Big O, Big Omega, Big Theta

body.en:
Asymptotic notations are mathematical tools that describe the growth rate of an algorithm's running time when the input size n becomes very large. Constants and lower-order terms are ignored, because for large n only the highest-order term matters.

1. Big O notation (upper bound)

f(n) = O(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that

f(n) ≤ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

  • g(n) is an upper bound: the algorithm takes at most this much time.
  • Used to express the worst case. It is the most widely used notation.
  • Example: 3n + 2 = O(n), because 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for all n ≥ 2 (c = 4, n₀ = 2).

2. Big Omega (Ω) notation (lower bound)

f(n) = Ω(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c and n₀ such that

f(n) ≥ c · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

  • g(n) is a lower bound: the algorithm takes at least this much time.
  • Used to express the best case.
  • Example: 3n + 2 = Ω(n), because 3n + 2 ≥ 3n for all n ≥ 1 (c = 3, n₀ = 1).

3. Big Theta (Θ) notation (tight bound)

f(n) = Θ(g(n)) if there exist positive constants c₁, c₂ and n₀ such that

c₁ · g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂ · g(n) for all n ≥ n₀

  • g(n) is both an upper and a lower bound: an exact (tight) growth rate.
  • Often used for the average case.
  • Example: 3n + 2 = Θ(n), because 3n ≤ 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for all n ≥ 2.
NotationBoundMeaningCase
OUpperat mostWorst
ΩLowerat leastBest
ΘTightexactlyAverage

Rules for finding Big O quickly

  • Drop constants: O(5n) = O(n).
  • Keep only the largest term: O(n² + 3n + 7) = O(n²).
  • Consecutive blocks add: O(n) + O(n²) = O(n²).
  • Nested blocks multiply: a loop of n inside a loop of n = O(n × n) = O(n²).

h.en: 1.4.1 Array: Definition and Representation in Memory

body.en:
An array is a finite, ordered collection of homogeneous (same type) elements stored in contiguous memory locations and referred to by a common name. Each element is accessed with an index (subscript).

/* 5 ints        */
int marks[5];
float price[3] = {9.5, 12, 7.25};
char name[20] = "GTU";
int a[] = {4, 8, 15, 16, 23};  /* size 5 */

Features of arrays

  • Homogeneous: all elements have the same data type.
  • Contiguous: elements are stored side by side in memory.
  • Fixed size: the size is decided at declaration and cannot change (static).
  • Indexed: in C the index starts from 0 (lower bound LB = 0) and ends at size − 1 (upper bound UB).
  • Random access: any element can be reached directly in O(1) time using its index.

Number of elements (length)

Length = UB − LB + 1. For A[5..50], length = 50 − 5 + 1 = 46.

Address of an element in a 1-D array

Because the elements are contiguous, the address of any element can be calculated from the address of the first element (the base address):

LOC(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB)

  • Base = address of the first element
  • w = size of one element in bytes (word size)
  • LB = lower bound of the index (0 in C)

Example: int A[6], base = 1000, w = 4. LOC(A[2]) = 1000 + 4 × (2 − 0) = 1008.

h.en: 1.4.2 Two-Dimensional Arrays: Row Major and Column Major

body.en:
A 2-D array stores elements in the form of a table (matrix) of M rows and N columns. It has M × N elements.

int m[2][3] = { {1, 2, 3},
                /* 2 rows, 3 cols */
                {4, 5, 6} };
printf("%d", m[1][2]);         /* 6 */

Memory, however, is one-dimensional (a single line of bytes). The table is therefore stored in one of two orders:

1. Row major order

  • Elements are stored row by row: all elements of row 0, then all of row 1, and so on.
  • Used by C, C++, Java and Python.
  • For a matrix [[a b c],[d e f]] the memory order is: a b c d e f.

LOC(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [ (i − Lr) × N + (j − Lc) ]

2. Column major order

  • Elements are stored column by column: all elements of column 0, then column 1, and so on.
  • Used by FORTRAN, MATLAB and R.
  • For the same matrix the memory order is: a d b e c f.

LOC(A[i][j]) = Base + w × [ (j − Lc) × M + (i − Lr) ]

where M = number of rows, N = number of columns, Lr = lower bound of rows, Lc = lower bound of columns, w = element size.

If the bounds are given as A[Lr..Ur][Lc..Uc], then M = Ur − Lr + 1 and N = Uc − Lc + 1.

Row majorColumn major
Row by rowColumn by column
Uses N (columns) in the formulaUses M (rows) in the formula
C, C++, JavaFORTRAN, MATLAB
a b c d e fa d b e c f

Tip: in row major, to reach row i you skip i complete rows of N elements each. In column major, to reach column j you skip j complete columns of M elements each.

h.en: 1.4.3 Advantages, Disadvantages and Applications of Arrays

body.en:
Advantages

  • Random access: any element is accessed in O(1) time with its index.
  • Simple to declare and use; many items with one name.
  • Easy traversal with a loop; good for sorting and searching (binary search needs an array).
  • No extra memory for links (unlike a linked list).
  • Used to implement other structures: stack, queue, heap, hash table, matrix.

Disadvantages

  • Fixed size: must be known in advance; cannot grow or shrink at run time.
  • Memory wastage if fewer elements are stored than declared; overflow if more are needed.
  • Insertion and deletion are slow (O(n)), because elements must be shifted.
  • Only homogeneous elements can be stored.
  • Needs a contiguous block of memory, which may not be available for very large arrays.

Applications

  • Storing lists of data: marks, salaries, temperatures.
  • Matrices and tables (2-D arrays), images (pixels).
  • Implementing stack, queue, heap and hash tables.
  • Lookup tables, sorting and searching algorithms.
  • CPU scheduling tables and database records.

title.en: 1.5 Array Operations: Traverse, Insert, Delete, Update, Search

body.en:
Traversing means accessing (visiting) each element exactly once in order to process it: print it, add it to a sum, count it, find the maximum, etc.

Algorithm TRAVERSE(A, LB, UB)
Step 1: Set K = LB
Step 2: Repeat while K <= UB
            Process A[K]   (e.g. print)
            Set K = K + 1
        [End of loop]
Step 3: Exit
  • Number of steps = number of elements = n.
  • Time complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) extra.

Applications: displaying elements, sum and average, maximum and minimum, counting even/odd numbers, reversing an array.

Insertion adds a new element at a given position. Since array elements are contiguous, all elements from that position to the end must first be shifted one place to the right to create space.

  • Shifting must start from the last element and move backwards. Starting from the front would overwrite values.
  • Before inserting, check for overflow (array already full, N = MAX).
Algorithm INSERT(A, N, POS, ITEM)
Step 1: [Check overflow]
        If N = MAX then
            Write "Overflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set J = N - 1
Step 3: Repeat while J >= POS
            Set A[J + 1] = A[J]
            Set J = J - 1
        [End of loop]
Step 4: Set A[POS] = ITEM
Step 5: Set N = N + 1
Step 6: Exit

(POS here is the array index, starting from 0.)

Complexity

  • Best case O(1): insert at the end, no shifting.
  • Worst case O(n): insert at the beginning, all n elements shift.
  • Average case O(n): about n/2 shifts.

Inserting into a sorted array: start from the end, shift every element larger than the new item one place right, then place the item in the gap.

Deletion removes the element at a given position. All the elements after it are shifted one place to the left to fill the gap, and the number of elements N is reduced by 1.

  • Shifting starts from the element just after the deleted position and moves forward.
  • Before deleting, check for underflow (array empty, N = 0).
Algorithm DELETE(A, N, POS)
Step 1: [Check underflow]
        If N = 0 then
            Write "Underflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set ITEM = A[POS]
Step 3: Repeat for J = POS to N - 2
            Set A[J] = A[J + 1]
        [End of loop]
Step 4: Set N = N - 1
Step 5: Write ITEM deleted
Step 6: Exit

Complexity

  • Best case O(1): delete the last element.
  • Worst case O(n): delete the first element, n − 1 elements shift.
  • Average case O(n).

Deleting by value means first searching for the value (O(n)) and then deleting at that position.

Update (modify) changes the value of an existing element. No shifting is needed and the number of elements does not change.

Algorithm UPDATE(A, N, POS, NEW)
Step 1: If POS < 0 or POS >= N then
            Write "Invalid" and Exit
Step 2: Set A[POS] = NEW
Step 3: Exit
  • Update by index: a single assignment A[POS] = NEW → O(1).
  • Update by value: first search for the old value (O(n)), then replace it → O(n).

Searching finds the location (index or position) of an element with a given value, called the key. The search is successful if the key is found, and unsuccessful otherwise.

Linear (sequential) search

The key is compared with every element, one by one from the first, until it is found or the array ends.

Algorithm LSEARCH(A, N, KEY)
Step 1: Set I = 0, LOC = -1
Step 2: Repeat while I < N
            If A[I] = KEY then
                Set LOC = I, go to Step 3
            Set I = I + 1
        [End of loop]
Step 3: If LOC = -1 then
            Write "Not found"
        Else
            Write "Found at", LOC + 1
Step 4: Exit
  • Works on unsorted and sorted arrays.
  • Best case O(1), worst case O(n), average about n/2 comparisons → O(n).

Binary search (Unit 5) works only on sorted arrays. It repeatedly halves the search range, giving O(log n).

Summary of array operations

OperationBestWorst
Access by indexO(1)O(1)
TraverseO(n)O(n)
InsertO(1) at endO(n) at start
DeleteO(1) at endO(n) at start
Update by indexO(1)O(1)
Linear searchO(1)O(n)

title.en: Maximum of 10 numbers using an array (with time complexity) [Practical 1]

programs.out:
Enter 10 numbers:
12 45 7 89 23 56 34 91 18 60
Maximum = 91
Comparisons = 9
Time complexity = O(n)

expl.en:
• The first element is taken as the maximum. Each of the remaining n − 1 elements is compared once with max.
  • The counter proves it: for n = 10 there are exactly 9 comparisons.
  • The number of steps grows in direct proportion to n, so the time complexity is O(n) (linear). It is the same in the best, average and worst case, because every element must be checked.
  • Space complexity: array of n elements + 4 variables → O(n); extra space apart from the input is O(1).

title.en: Primitive data types and their sizes

programs.out:
Type  B Value
int   4 25
float 4 3.5
dbl   8 3.14159
char  1 A
ptr   8 25

expl.en:
• These are primitive data structures: the basic types that the machine works on directly. Each holds a single value.
  • Sizes depend on the compiler and machine. On a 64-bit GCC system an int is 4 bytes, a double 8 bytes and a pointer 8 bytes. On Turbo C (16-bit) an int is 2 bytes.
  • Non-primitive structures such as arrays, stacks and linked lists are built from these primitive types.

title.en: Counting steps: O(n), O(n²) and O(log n) loops

expl.en:
• Single loop: the body runs n times → O(n). Doubling n doubles the count.
  • Nested loop: n × n runs → O(n²). Doubling n makes the count four times bigger (64 → 256 → 1024 → 4096).
  • Doubling loop (i = i * 2): i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8 … so it runs log₂n times → O(log n). Even for n = 64 it runs only 6 times.
  • This is exactly how the frequency count method finds time complexity: count how many times the key statement executes as a function of n.

title.en: Traversing an array with addresses (contiguous memory)

programs.out:
Index Value Offset
a[0]    15     0
a[1]     7     4
a[2]    42     8
a[3]     9    12
a[4]    23    16
a[5]    31    20
Sum = 127
a[i] at base + 4 * i

expl.en:
• Traversing means visiting every element exactly once. Here each element is printed and added to sum.
  • The offset column shows the distance of each element from the start of the array. It goes up by 4 bytes (the size of an int), which proves the elements are stored in contiguous (side-by-side) memory.
  • So the address of a[i] = base address + 4 × i. This is the formula LOC(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB) with LB = 0.
  • (Real addresses change on every run, so only the offsets are printed.) Time complexity of traversal: O(n).

title.en: Insert an element at a given position

programs.out:
Enter number of elements: 5
Enter 5 elements: 10 20 30 40 50
Position (1-6): 3
Enter element to insert: 25
Array after insertion: 10 20 25 30 40 50

expl.en:
• The user gives the position from 1, so the array index is pos − 1.
  • Elements from the last one down to index pos − 1 are shifted one place right. The loop must run from the end; shifting from the front would overwrite values.
  • The new item is then placed in the free slot and n is increased by 1.
  • The check n == MAX prevents overflow (no free space).
  • Complexity: best case O(1) (insert at the end), worst case O(n) (insert at the beginning, all n elements shift).

title.en: Delete an element from a given position

programs.out:
Enter number of elements: 6
Enter 6 elements: 10 20 25 30 40 50
Delete position (1-6): 2
Deleted element = 20
Array after deletion: 10 25 30 40 50

expl.en:
• The element at index pos − 1 is saved in item, so it can be reported.
  • All elements after it move one place left, starting from the front. This closes the gap.
  • n is reduced by 1. The old last slot still holds a value, but it is no longer part of the array.
  • n == 0 means the array is empty (underflow).
  • Complexity: best case O(1) (delete the last element), worst case O(n) (delete the first element).

title.en: Update (replace) a value in an array

programs.out:
Array: 10 20 30 40 50 
Enter value to update: 30
Enter new value: 35
Updated a[2]
Array: 10 20 35 40 50

expl.en:
• Update changes the value of an existing element. No shifting is needed, so the array size stays the same.
  • If the index is known, the update is a single statement a[i] = new; → O(1).
  • If only the value is known (as here), it must first be searched → O(n) in the worst case.

programs.out:
Enter element to search: 90
90 found at position 5
Comparisons = 5

expl.en:
• Linear search compares the key with each element one by one, from the first element onwards.
  • The search stops at the first match. If the loop ends with i == n, the key is not present.
  • Here 90 is the 5th element, so 5 comparisons are needed.
  • Best case O(1): the key is the first element. Worst case O(n): the key is the last element or absent. Average ≈ n/2 comparisons → O(n).
  • It works on unsorted arrays too. Binary search (Unit 5) is faster but needs a sorted array.

title.en: Insert a value into a sorted array (keeps order)

programs.out:
Sorted array: 5 12 18 27 33 41 
Enter value to insert: 20
New array: 5 12 18 20 27 33 41

expl.en:
• The position does not need to be given. Starting from the end, every element bigger than the new item is shifted one place right.
  • When a smaller (or equal) element is found, or the start is reached, the item goes into the gap at i + 1.
  • The array stays sorted after insertion. This same idea is the heart of insertion sort (Unit 5).
  • Worst case O(n), when the new item is the smallest.

title.en: Row major and column major order of a matrix

programs.out:
Matrix:
  1  2  3
  4  5  6
Memory order in C: 1 2 3 4 5 6 
Row major order   : 1 2 3 4 5 6 
Column major order: 1 4 2 5 3 6

expl.en:
• A 2-D array is a table, but memory is a single line of bytes, so the table must be linearised.
  • Reading memory directly through a pointer (p[0] … p[5]) gives 1 2 3 4 5 6: C stores arrays in row major order (row 0 first, then row 1).
  • Row major: outer loop on rows, inner loop on columns. Column major: outer loop on columns, inner loop on rows → 1 4 2 5 3 6 (used by FORTRAN and MATLAB).

title.en: Address calculation: 1-D, row major and column major

programs.out:
1-D: base w LB i: 2000 2 0 23
A[23] = 2046
2-D: base w LR LC M N: 1000 4 1 1 4 5
Find A[i][j], enter i j: 3 4
Row major    = 1052
Column major = 1056

expl.en:
• 1-D: LOC(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB). For base 2000, w = 2, LB = 0, i = 23 → 2000 + 46 = 2046.
  • 2-D: array A[1..4][1..5] (M = 4 rows, N = 5 columns), base 1000, w = 4, find A[3][4]:
    Row major = 1000 + 4 × [(3−1) × 5 + (4−1)] = 1000 + 4 × 13 = 1052
    Column major = 1000 + 4 × [(4−1) × 4 + (3−1)] = 1000 + 4 × 14 = 1056
  • In row major, the number of columns N is used (whole rows are skipped). In column major, the number of rows M is used (whole columns are skipped).

• The first and last elements are swapped, then the second and second-last, and so on, until the middle is reached.
  • Only n / 2 swaps are needed (3 swaps for 7 elements; the middle element stays in place).
  • Time complexity O(n). Only one extra variable t is used, so the extra space is O(1). This is called an in-place algorithm.

title.en: Largest and second largest in one traversal

expl.en:
• Sorting first would cost O(n log n) or O(n²). A single traversal does the job in O(n), a better algorithm for the same problem.
  • When a new largest is found, the old largest moves down to second.
  • a[i] != first skips duplicates of the largest (89 appears twice), so the answer is 78 and not 89.
  • INT_MIN (from limits.h) is the smallest int, a safe starting value.

title.en: Insertion and Deletion in an Array

items.f:
Algorithm MAX(A, N)
A = array of N elements, MAX = largest
Step 1: [Initialize]  Set MAX = A[0]
Step 2: [Loop]  Repeat for I = 1 to N-1
            If A[I] > MAX then
                Set MAX = A[I]
        [End of loop]
Step 3: [Output]  Print MAX
Step 4: Exit

Algorithm TRAVERSE(A, LB, UB)
Step 1: Set K = LB
Step 2: Repeat while K <= UB
            Process A[K]   (e.g. print)
            Set K = K + 1
        [End of loop]
Step 3: Exit

Algorithm INSERT(A, N, POS, ITEM)
Step 1: [Check overflow]
        If N = MAX then
            Write "Overflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set J = N - 1
Step 3: Repeat while J >= POS
            Set A[J + 1] = A[J]
            Set J = J - 1
        [End of loop]
Step 4: Set A[POS] = ITEM
Step 5: Set N = N + 1
Step 6: Exit

terms.en: Shift right from the end. Worst O(n).

items.f:
Algorithm DELETE(A, N, POS)
Step 1: [Check underflow]
        If N = 0 then
            Write "Underflow" and Exit
Step 2: Set ITEM = A[POS]
Step 3: Repeat for J = POS to N - 2
            Set A[J] = A[J + 1]
        [End of loop]
Step 4: Set N = N - 1
Step 5: Write ITEM deleted
Step 6: Exit

terms.en: Shift left from POS + 1. Worst O(n).

items.f:
Algorithm UPDATE(A, N, POS, NEW)
Step 1: If POS < 0 or POS >= N then
            Write "Invalid" and Exit
Step 2: Set A[POS] = NEW
Step 3: Exit

Algorithm LSEARCH(A, N, KEY)
Step 1: Set I = 0, LOC = -1
Step 2: Repeat while I < N
            If A[I] = KEY then
                Set LOC = I, go to Step 3
            Set I = I + 1
        [End of loop]
Step 3: If LOC = -1 then
            Write "Not found"
        Else
            Write "Found at", LOC + 1
Step 4: Exit

LOC(A[i]) = Base + w*(i - LB)
Length  = UB - LB + 1

terms.en: w = element size, LB = lower bound.
N = number of columns. Used by C.
M = number of rows. Used by FORTRAN.

A 2-D array A[10][20] (indexes start from 0) has base address 100 and each element needs 2 bytes. Find the address of A[5][8] using (i) row major and (ii) column major order.

a.en:
StatementCount

Highest-order term is n → O(n).

For n = 10: 2 × 10 + 3 = 23 steps.

q.en: Find the time complexity of: for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < i; j++) count++; How many times does count++ run for n = 10?

a.en:
For each value of i, the inner loop runs i times:

i = 0 → 0, i = 1 → 1, i = 2 → 2, …, i = n − 1 → n − 1

Total = 0 + 1 + 2 + … + (n − 1) = n(n − 1) / 2 = (n² − n)/2

Highest-order term n²/2 → O(n²).

For n = 10: 10 × 9 / 2 = 45 times.

q.en: Find the time complexity of: i = 1; while (i < n) i = i * 2; How many iterations for n = 64 and n = 1000?

a.en:
i takes the values 1, 2, 4, 8, …, 2ᵏ. The loop stops when 2ᵏ ≥ n, i.e. after k = ⌈log₂ n⌉ iterations.

Time complexity = O(log n).

n = 64: i = 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 → 6 iterations (log₂ 64 = 6).

n = 1000: 2⁹ = 512 < 1000 ≤ 2¹⁰ = 1024 → 10 iterations.

q.en: Show that f(n) = 3n + 2 is O(n), Ω(n) and Θ(n).

a.en:
Big O: 3n + 2 ≤ 3n + n = 4n when n ≥ 2. So f(n) ≤ 4·n for all n ≥ 2 → c = 4, n₀ = 2 → f(n) = O(n).

Big Ω: 3n + 2 ≥ 3n for all n ≥ 1 → c = 3, n₀ = 1 → f(n) = Ω(n).

Big Θ: combining both, 3n ≤ 3n + 2 ≤ 4n for all n ≥ 2 → c₁ = 3, c₂ = 4, n₀ = 2 → f(n) = Θ(n).

q.en: Show that f(n) = 10n² + 4n + 2 is O(n²). Find suitable c and n₀.

a.en:
Try c = 11: we need 10n² + 4n + 2 ≤ 11n², i.e. 4n + 2 ≤ n².

n4n + 2n²holds?
41816No
52225Yes
62636Yes

For all n ≥ 5 the condition holds (n² grows faster than 4n + 2).

So 10n² + 4n + 2 ≤ 11n² for n ≥ 5 → c = 11, n₀ = 5 → f(n) = O(n²).

(Also 10n² + 4n + 2 ≥ 10n² for n ≥ 1, so f(n) = Ω(n²) and hence Θ(n²).)

q.en: Find the memory needed for int A[10][20] if an int takes 4 bytes. What is the space complexity of adding two n × n matrices into a third matrix?

a.en:
Number of elements = 10 × 20 = 200. Memory = 200 × 4 = 800 bytes.

Matrix addition C = A + B for n × n matrices needs 3 matrices of n² elements each, plus the loop variables i, j and n (fixed part).

S(P) = 3n² + 3 → O(n²).

q.en: What is a data structure?

a.en: A way of organising and storing data in memory so that it can be accessed and modified efficiently.

q.en: Differentiate data and information.

a.en: Data are raw facts with no meaning (e.g. marks). Information is processed, meaningful data (e.g. result, average).

q.en: What are primitive data structures? Give examples.

a.en: Basic types operated directly by machine instructions and holding a single value: int, float, char, double, pointer.

q.en: What are non-primitive data structures?

a.en: Structures derived from primitive types that store a collection of values: array, stack, queue, linked list, tree, graph.

q.en: Differentiate linear and non-linear data structures.

a.en: Linear: elements in a sequence, traversed in one run (array, stack, queue, list). Non-linear: hierarchy or network (tree, graph).

q.en: Is a stack linear or non-linear?

a.en: Linear. Its elements are kept in a sequence, though insertion and deletion happen only at the top.

q.en: What is the difference between static and dynamic data structures?

a.en: Static: size fixed at compile time (array). Dynamic: size changes at run time (linked list).

q.en: List the common operations on data structures.

a.en: Traversing, searching, insertion, deletion, sorting and merging.

q.en: What is an algorithm?

a.en: A finite sequence of well-defined steps that solves a problem, taking input and producing output in finite time.

q.en: State the characteristics of an algorithm.

a.en: Input, output, definiteness, finiteness and effectiveness.

q.en: What is time complexity?

a.en: The amount of time an algorithm needs as a function of input size n, measured by counting basic operations.

q.en: What is space complexity?

a.en: The amount of memory an algorithm needs as a function of n: fixed part + variable part.

q.en: What is the frequency count method?

a.en: Counting how many times each statement executes and adding them to get the total steps as a function of n.

q.en: What is Big O notation?

a.en: An upper bound on growth: f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. It gives the worst case.

q.en: What is Big Omega notation?

a.en: A lower bound: f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀. It gives the best case.

q.en: What is Big Theta notation?

a.en: A tight bound: c₁·g(n) ≤ f(n) ≤ c₂·g(n). Both upper and lower bound.

q.en: What is the time complexity of a nested loop of n inside n?

a.en: O(n²).

q.en: Which is faster: O(n log n) or O(n²)?

a.en: O(n log n). For large n it grows much more slowly.

q.en: What are the best and worst cases of linear search?

a.en: Best O(1) (key at the first position), worst O(n) (key at the end or absent).

q.en: What is an array?

a.en: A finite collection of same-type elements stored in contiguous memory under one name and accessed by index.

q.en: Why does the array index start at 0 in C?

a.en: The index is the offset from the base address: a[i] is at base + i × w, so the first element has offset 0.

q.en: Give the address formula for a 1-D array.

a.en: LOC(A[i]) = Base + w × (i − LB).

q.en: What is row major order?

a.en: Storing a 2-D array row by row. C uses it.

q.en: What is column major order?

a.en: Storing a 2-D array column by column. FORTRAN uses it.

q.en: Why are insertion and deletion slow in arrays?

a.en: Elements must be shifted to make or close a gap, which takes O(n) time.

q.en: What is overflow and underflow in an array?

a.en: Overflow: inserting into a full array. Underflow: deleting from an empty array.

q.en: Give two disadvantages of arrays.

a.en: Fixed size (wastage or overflow) and slow insertion and deletion.
